_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Priya Nakamura, senior policy analyst, state health benefit exchange
reinforcement_note: All 6 target Calculus/Limits And Continuity skills already carry n=1 in readmodel/standards_spine.json as of this write pass (2026-09-01) — a single existing case is the only thing covering the entire group, a structural single-point-of-failure risk flagged by the concept sheet's addendum. This case does not open new_coverage (per SPEC §4's strict n==0 definition); instead it independently reinforces every one of the 6 skills twice — once via Hold The Cliff (D1-D2) and once via Build The Bridge (D3), each requiring the full one-sided-limit-to-continuity-test chain on different data — moving the group from n=1 to n=3 per skill and removing the single-point-of-failure risk. See LEARNING_GOALS.md coverage note for the full argument. This is an explicit, instructed write-time exception to the usual non-empty-new_coverage requirement.

deliverables.text: A piecewise definition of the net cost function, plus both one-sided limits at the threshold, for Hold The Cliff — computed algebraically from Appendix A's threshold and Appendix B's household cost figures.
A continuity test at the threshold for Hold The Cliff, applying the three-part definition of continuity at a point, stating which part fails and naming the resulting discontinuity.

The same two computations (piecewise definition, one-sided limits, continuity test) for Build The Bridge using Appendix C's continuous formula, showing explicitly whether it passes where Hold The Cliff failed.

A discontinuity-size-versus-cost table: the dollar size of the D1-D2 jump discontinuity under Hold The Cliff, versus Build The Bridge's real annual cost to the state, scaled using Appendix D and Appendix E figures.
A recommendation memo stating which option Priya should recommend, defended against the discretionary line item and the budget markup deadline in Appendix E.

The Cost of Closing the Gap
Priya's State: Enrollment, Budget Line, and Deadline

balance.argument_a: Hold The Cliff costs the state $0 against a $8,000,000 one-time discretionary line item that stays fully available for other priorities, and it requires zero new administrative rule — the exchange simply applies the published federal formula. Real per-state wraparound programs run $21.5M-$300M a year (Appendix D); this state's estimated ~14,400 near-threshold households (3% of 480,000 enrollees, Appendix E) would need an ongoing appropriation on that same order, which the one-time $8M line item cannot fund at all. Even setting the funding-mechanism problem aside, Build The Bridge's real per-household cost ($9,491) is 7.74% higher than the $8,756 discontinuity it removes (Appendix B/C) — a real, computed, quantitative edge for A, not just an administrative-simplicity argument.
balance.argument_b: Build The Bridge is provably continuous at the threshold — the same left-limit-equals-right-limit-equals-function-value check that Hold The Cliff fails comes out clean under Appendix C's formula — and real states (New Mexico, Massachusetts, California) have already judged a version of this kind of smoothing worth funding at real, named dollar costs. But 'worth funding' is not 'free': the real per-state costs in Appendix D, and the CBO's ≈$350B/10yr federal-scale estimate for a permanent nationwide version of this same fix, show the state cost is a genuine, recurring budget line, not a rounding error.
balance.margin_basis: Compare (a) the dollar size of the D1/D2 jump discontinuity under Hold The Cliff, scaled by the D4 estimate of how many of this state's households sit close enough to the threshold to fall into it, against (b) Build The Bridge's real annual state cost (Appendix D/E), once Appendix A-E's NEEDS_SOURCE figures are resolved by case-research. The case is NOT asking which option is mathematically cleaner — B provably wins that, per D2/D3 — it is asking whether the total dollar harm of the discontinuity, at this state's actual scale, is large enough relative to Build The Bridge's real cost to justify the spend, which only resolves once both sides are computed.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Scaled to the rough size of a real, comparably-sized state-based marketplace (Pennsylvania's Pennie, ~486,000 enrollees at close of 2026 OE, S16). Priya's state is deliberately not identified with any real state.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Pure scale factor — multiplies both the harm side and the cost side of D4 equally, so it does not change which option wins, only the headline dollar totals.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Share of enrollees within reach of the 400%-FPL threshold
modeling_assumptions.basis: Uses the national 400-500% FPL band share (S15) as the nearest published proxy for 'close enough to the threshold that a modest income change crosses it.' No dataset publishes a narrower band.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Least-defensible figure in the case; the true 'near the line' population is likely smaller than this 3% band. However, this factor cancels out of the per-household margin used for the D4/D5 recommendation (see FACILITATOR.md), so it does not by itself flip the recommendation — it only changes both totals' scale together.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Discretionary budget line item available this cycle
modeling_assumptions.basis: Set well below any real per-state wraparound program's ongoing annual cost in Appendix D (New Mexico ~$38.8M, Massachusetts $250M, California $190M-$300M), consistent with Background's framing of this as a one-time discretionary item, not an ongoing appropriation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The sharpest lever in the case. If large enough to cover Build The Bridge's real annual cost outright, the budget-feasibility objection to Option B disappears. At $8M one-time, it cannot fund an ongoing subsidy program at this state's estimated scale, which is a decisive practical objection to B in this budget cycle regardless of the D4 cost-effectiveness margin.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Illustrative narrative urgency from the Overview; not derived from a real legislative calendar.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not affect D1-D4 math. Bears only on D5's practical argument for A as the option requiring no new administrative process before a near-term deadline.

per_household.note: 8,756 = 14,931 - 6,175 (Appendix B, S3). 5,440 = 0.085 x 64,000 (Appendix C's 8.5% cap applied to Household 2's income). 9,491 = 14,931 - 5,440 (state cost to bring Household 2 down to the capped rate).

No vote at Anchor 1 -- Priya's opening position is stated instead of voted. The guide plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands; 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why.'

sensitivity_note: This case touches real, current (2026) health-policy and federal-budget debate — the ACA premium subsidy 400%-FPL cliff and its federal deficit cost. Per SPEC §6, framing must stay strictly on the neutral, computable analytical question (the real, calculable size of a discontinuity in a household cost function, and the real, named cost of removing it) rather than on which policy position is "correct." FACILITATOR.md carries this flag explicitly for any facilitator running the discussion. No real state currently extends smoothing above 400% FPL; Build The Bridge is written as a policy option grounded in real state precedent for lower income bands, not as an already-implemented program — Background states this explicitly.
